basic_info.title: Which Tasks Should Be Learned Together in Multi-task Learning?

method.notes: Shows empirically that tasks sharing a network compete for representation capacity, and that which tasks cooperate vs. compete cannot be reliably predicted from task similarity alone -- some pairs help each other, others actively hurt each other's accuracy when trained jointly, depending on gradient geometry and capacity allocation. Proposes a framework to search for which task GROUPINGS to co-train vs. separate. Directly explains the 'hit@1 degrades while cl_gps improves with continued Stage-2 training' pattern found in evaluation_findings.md: the MDN GPS reconstruction head (dense, continuous, high-gradient-bandwidth) and the RoadScorer head (discrete CE, likely lower/sparser gradient signal) share the same (h,z) representation, and this paper's finding is that such asymmetric-bandwidth task pairs progressively favor the stronger task as training proceeds -- exactly the observed degradation.

gap_analysis.whats_missing: Not a map-matching or pillar-novelty paper -- included as the literature explanation for a specific Stage-2 training pathology (road quality degrading while GPS quality improves).
gap_analysis.novelty_reasoning: Relevant only as the general multi-task-learning finding that explains why two heads sharing (h,z) can progressively diverge in training quality without either being 'broken'.

relevance.bmw_relevance: Not directly BMW-relevant; cited to correctly frame the newly observed 'hit@1 degrades while cl_gps improves' pattern (Change-13 evaluation) as ordinary multi-task gradient competition/negative transfer between the MDN GPS head and RoadScorer head, not a novel or RSSM-specific failure mode requiring its own bespoke fix.

uncertain: The paper's task-grouping search method itself (branch-and-bound over task-assignment trees) was not evaluated for direct applicability to Stage-2's two-head setup -- cited only for its diagnostic framing, not as a proposed algorithmic fix.
